canberra.title: Inflation eases just as fuel excise discount about to end
canberra.snippet: Inflation eased last month more than anticipated, with the consumer price index rising 3.8 per cent in the 12 months to June, which is do...
canberra.content:
Fuel excise will return to normal on Monday (3 August). Photo: David Murtagh.

Inflation eased last month more than anticipated, with the consumer price index rising 3.8 per cent in the 12 months to June, which is down from 4 per cent the previous month.

Most economists had forecast inflation to be higher.

Australian Bureau of Statistics data shows the largest contributor to annual inflation in June was housing, which rose by 6.8 per cent, with the next largest contributors being food and non-alcoholic beverages, and recreation and culture, which both rose by 3.3 per cent.

Annual housing inflation of 6.8 per cent in the 12 months to June reflects rising costs for electricity and new dwellings.

ABS head of price statistics Rachael McCririck said that looking through some of the bigger price movements, underlying inflation was steady at 3.6 per cent in the 12 months to June 2026, the same as in the 12 months to May.

“Electricity remains one of the biggest contributors to annual inflation, with costs 22.4 per cent higher than 12 months ago,” Ms McCririck said.

“This is largely because government rebates, which reduced household electricity bills, have ended.

“Annual inflation for new dwellings has reached its highest level in almost three years, at 5.8 per cent. This was driven by builders passing on higher material and labour costs.”

When prices for some items change significantly, she said, the trimmed mean (a statistical measure that removes a set percentage of the largest and smallest values from a dataset before calculating the final mean) can give more insights into how underlying inflation is trending without the impact of temporary shocks.

For example, automotive fuel has been excluded from the trimmed mean every month since March 2026 when the Middle East war hit fuel prices.

Annual inflation for transport has moderated, recording a 0.1 per cent rise, down from a 3.3 per cent rise in May.

This was driven by automotive fuel prices falling for three consecutive months between April and June 2026.

“Lower world oil prices as a result of some stabilisation in the Middle East in June contributed to fuel prices falling 10.9 per cent in the month,” Ms McCririck said.

“The Federal Government’s fuel excise relief measures, which contributed to lower automotive fuel prices in April and May, also remained in place.”

But Treasurer Jim Chalmers has confirmed the fuel excise discount will be gone by Monday (3 August).

The cut took 16 cents off each litre of fuel as a measure to ease the financial impacts of the Middle East war and fuel supply issues.

“That fuel excise relief will end midnight on Sunday and that’s because it has played a really important role helping to take some of the sting out of these cost-of-living pressures,” Dr Chalmers said.

“It was never the government’s intention for that to be permanent. We began to taper that off at the start of the month, deliberately, so that we could provide a bit more cost of living help.”

Speaking specifically on inflation, the Treasurer said that while the latest CPI figure is lower than was forecast, it remains higher than the Federal Government wants.

“This is the third consecutive month now where annual headline inflation has come down,” he said.

“It is an encouraging outcome that shows that we have made some progress on inflation since the budget… [but] we know that people are still under pressure.

“We know that inflation is still higher than we would like it to be. We know that the war in the Middle East and the uncertain developments, even in the last couple of weeks, risk that outlook as well.

“But in the circumstances that we find ourselves in, these numbers today are encouraging.”

The latest data has tempered forecasts for another Reserve Bank rate rise next month, with financial markets all but ruling it out.

Nevertheless, the Greens have used the data to repeat their call for a rent freeze for the next 12 months and a moratorium on no-cause evictions.

They point to housing costs driving inflation, with the cost of living remaining too expensive for Australian households.

“High inflation means that too many households are just one rent increase away from eviction or homelessness,” Greens housing spokesperson Barbara Pocock said.

“A rent freeze and ban on evictions will give people more security in a cost of living and fuel crisis. Households across the country are already doing it tough.”

canberra.title: Voters not impressed with Taylor, One Nation, AI, or Labor on inflation, polling shows
canberra.snippet: Australians don’t much care for how Labor is handling the economy at the moment, but they prefer the government to anything else on offer...
canberra.content:
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor’s approval rating has dived, according to the latest Essential Poll. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

Australians don’t much care for how Labor is handling the economy at the moment, but they prefer the government to anything else on offer, according to the latest opinion polling.

The Essential Poll, commissioned by The Guardian, shows support for both the Coalition and One Nation has dipped, while Opposition Leader Angus Taylor’s approval rating is in freefall.

The poll was undertaken last week of 1060 demographically weighted voters and found One Nation’s recent meteoric rise seems to be over.

The party attracted a 25 per cent primary vote, which is down 1 point from June’s poll, slipping away from a high of 28 per cent it rated in May in the Essential survey.

The Coalition dropped another point from the last poll to 22 per cent, while Labor’s primary vote was up 1 point to 31 per cent.

But it’s Mr Taylor’s approval rating that is ringing alarm bells across the Coalition.

The Opposition Leader’s performance approval dropped 3 points from last month’s poll to 33 per cent and his disapproval rate shot up by 7 points to 44 per cent, resulting in a net approval of minus 11.

It dropped 13 points among voters aged 18 to 34 and 20 points among those aged 35 to 54.

His approval with men plummeted 16 points, whereas it only dropped 4 points among women.

Anthony Albanese’s approval rating isn’t great either, with 38 per cent approving of his performance as Prime Minister and 52 per cent disapproving.

That gives the PM a net approval rating of minus 14, up 1 from last month but continuing a 4-month streak of more than half of voters disapproving of his performance.

Labor has been marked down over its handling of inflation and the cost of living crisis, with a whopping 64 per cent of the pollster’s respondents rating its performance in that area as poor.

Only 16 per cent rated it as good.

Voters are also unhappy about the government’s embrace of artificial intelligence.

Only 28 per cent of respondents said they would support a new data centre being built in their area, while 37 per cent were against the idea.

A whopping 61 per cent of voters had concerns over AI’s demand for energy, and the impact that would have on power prices, while 44 per cent mentioned concerns for water supply.

Thirty-nine per cent of respondents said they were worried about AI in general, and another 41 per cent had concerns over environmental and noise pollution from AI data centres.

Men were split equally over AI, with 34 per cent supporting it and 34 per cent opposing, while more women disapproved of the new technology than approved of it, at 22 per cent and 39 per cent respectively.

Close to 80 per cent of respondents rated cost of living and inflation as one of the most important issues for them, followed by Medicare and health at 50 per cent, crime 42 per cent, and immigration 35 per cent.

In a recent landmark speech on the Federal Government’s approach to AI, Mr Albanese promised a national set of standards under one framework to ensure data centres don’t soak up energy supplies or impact power prices, or steal the work of local authors and creatives.

But the government is pushing ahead with positioning Australia as an attractive location for AI tech giants to invest.

The Prime Minister is establishing the Office of AI within his own department to coordinate a whole-of-government approach to the technology.

canberra.title: Government drops Arcadia House move to Cook, seeks new site
canberra.snippet: The proposed relocation of alcohol and drug rehabilitation services from the North Canberra Hospital campus to suburban Cook has been aba...
canberra.content:
29 July 2026

Join the conversation

7

The Cook town hall meeting on the Arcadia House relocation. Photo: Chiaka Barry/Facebook.

The proposed relocation of alcohol and drug rehabilitation services from the North Canberra Hospital campus to suburban Cook has been abandoned in the face of a community backlash.

The ACT Government announced the decision on Wednesday (29 July) after releasing a listening report from public consultation that found strong opposition to the proposed relocation of Directions Health Services’ Arcadia House to a site near Cook Oval, Cook Community Hub and shops.

The report also found a low level of trust among some community members in the consultation, with some questioning whether decisions had already been made and if the engagement process was genuine.

Opponents of the move said they supported the work of Arcadia House, but the two Cook sites considered were not appropriate.

They argued Cook should not lose any of its green space and such a facility should not be sited next to playgrounds, a childcare centre and licensed premises.

Canberra Liberals Chiaka Barry sponsored a petition against the proposal.

Health Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith said the decision to forgo Cook had been made on the basis of feedback about the current uses of the identified sites in Cook.

She rejected any suggestion that Arcadia House or its clients would have presented a risk to the surrounding community.

“Alcohol and drug rehabilitation services of this kind are best placed in the community and have an incentive to be excellent neighbours, which is exactly what we see with other sites across the ACT,” Ms Stephen-Smith said.

She thanked everyone who engaged in the consultation process, which involved two drop-in sessions, a community town hall, a stakeholder information session, 520 online survey submissions and 60 written submissions.

“At every stage, we were clear that no decision had been made regarding either site in Cook, and that community feedback would shape the next stage in the decision-making process,” Ms Stephen-Smith said.

The government remained committed to finding a permanent home for the service on the northside.

Infrastructure Canberra, in partnership with Directions ACT, is now assessing whether a potential alternative location has become available since the initial search or if any of the 60 previously considered sites warrant further investigation.

Technical investigations, planning requirements, environmental considerations and service delivery needs will inform the next stage of the process, with further consultation to be undertaken as required.

The government wants to relocate Arcadia House from the Bruce campus because the premises are ageing, no longer fit for purpose and will need to make way for the new Northside Hospital.

Arcadia House provides residential and day programs for people seeking to quit alcohol, tobacco and other drugs.

ACT Greens leader Jo Clay said the Cook community had been heard but the process was flawed.

“The listening report shows a significant proportion of Cook residents felt the decision was already made before consultation began,” she said.

“A procurement tender was underway before the survey even closed and trust was already fragile – the Cook school closure and broken promises about that site still matter here.

“This outcome is right. But the process was not good enough – and what comes next must be different.”

Ms Clay said Canberra still needed Arcadia House and the government must now find the right site, quickly and transparently, with the community genuinely involved from the very start.

canberra.title: Car left hanging from bridge as accident closes Princes Highway
canberra.snippet: A man has been rushed to hospital after his car was left hanging off a South Coast bridge. The accident happened on the Princes Highway n...
canberra.content:
29 July 2026

Start the conversation

The incident happened at about 8 am today (29 July). Image: LiveTraffic NSW.

A man has been rushed to hospital after his car was left hanging off a South Coast bridge.

The accident happened on the Princes Highway near Maulbrooks Road at Jeremadra, between Moruya and Batemans Bay, when a car towing a caravan went off the bridge at about 8 am (29 July).

A NSW Ambulance spokesperson said the man, aged in his 70s, was taken to Moruya Hospital in a stable condition.

“He managed to get out of the car,” they said.

A NSW Police spokesperson told Region police believe only one car was involved in the incident and the driver was the only occupant. Although they did not identify the driver, the caravan had ACT plates.

The highway was initially closed for several hours but has reopened to traffic.

As of 12.30 pm, travel on the Princes Highway remains affected.

According to Live Traffic NSW, alternating (stop/slow) traffic conditions are in place to allow motorists to pass in one direction at a time.

Original Article published by Claire Sams on About Regional.

australia.title: Mother went to South Australia police station day before suspected murder-suicide
australia.snippet: Police say chance of finding missing baby alive ‘zero’ after bodies of mother Helena Wright and toddler found in ocean near Port Macdonne...
australia.content:
A mother who died in a suspected murder-suicide went to the police station a day before the incident, South Australia police have confirmed.

The bodies of Helena Wright, 36, and her 23-month-old daughter were found in the ocean west of Port Macdonnell on Monday.

Police said on Wednesday afternoon they had ended the official search for a missing three-month-old after “careful consideration”, saying the infant “could not have survived the period of time that has elapsed, either in the water or on land”.

Emergency services were called to the area on Monday after a vehicle was found abandoned with its engine running at 11.15am.

Wright, originally from Estonia, had been living in Compton, a small locality outside Mount Gambier about 26km north of Port Macdonnell.

Police have confirmed Wright visited a police station the day before her body was discovered.

At about 9.30am on the day of the incident, officers conducted a welfare check at Wright’s home after a friend called police. Nobody was home at the time.

The mother and child were found below the cliffs and retrieved with help from local fishers.

Police have spoken to the woman’s husband, the father of the children, and said “based on the evidence currently available, the matter is being investigated as a murder-suicide”.

Land and sea searches around Cape Northumberland, near Port Macdonnell on the Limestone Coast, were conducted for the three-month-old.

“Comprehensive physical search efforts have focused on a sizeable area of water and land, unfortunately the infant has not been found,” police said on Wednesday.

They said hope of finding the infant alive was lost.

“The reality is, after three days, the chances of finding the baby alive are zero,” Supt Trent Cox said earlier on Wednesday.

Cox said extremely challenging conditions had hampered the search, forcing emergency vessels to stay out of the water for much of Tuesday and limiting efforts to shoreline and clifftop sweeps.

“We’ve been unable to … launch water assets. We’ve been able to get the SES aerial drone up,” he said, adding that experts had advised against deploying an underwater drone in the dangerous conditions.

Police they will continue to “coordinate shoreline monitoring and inspections across the coming days”.

The SA premier, Peter Malinauskas, said the tragedy had shocked the community.

“If it involves children, that breaks your heart,” he said on Tuesday.

The incident has been referred to the coroner to examine the cause and circumstances surrounding the deaths.

Police said “there is no information to suggest that any person other than the mother and her two children were involved in this heartbreaking incident”.

australia.title: Victorian cults inquiry accidentally shares email address of anonymous survivors with group members
australia.snippet: Committee apologises for not concealing email addresses when alerting witnesses to final report Get our breaking news email , free app or...
australia.content:
A Victorian parliamentary committee investigating the harmful impact of cults accidentally sent the email addresses of anonymous survivors who made submissions to current members of such groups and to journalists.

The committee, which had its report into “cults and organised fringe groups” tabled in parliament on Wednesday, emailed hundreds of recipients shortly after midday to inform them it had been published, but erroneously left their addresses visible.

“We would like to sincerely apologise for the email sent earlier today in which recipient email addresses were inadvertently included in the CC field,” the legal and social issues committee said, in a second email sent 42 minutes later.

“Due to an administrative technical error during the distribution process, the email was sent with visible recipient details. We understand the importance of protecting personal information and regret this mistake.

“To help minimise any further disclosure of information, we kindly ask that you delete the email from your inbox and any related folders (including Sent Items if applicable), and refrain from forwarding or sharing its contents. We appreciate your understanding and cooperation. We are reviewing our processes to help prevent a similar incident from occurring in the future.”

Karen Alsop, who publicly gave evidence to the committee about the Casey City church, said the email risked further traumatising people who lived with complex conditions including PTSD.

People belonging to groups accused of being cults during the inquiry were also included on the email, she said.

The survivors included whistleblowers who trusted they would remain anonymous even as they spoke out about their experiences.

“This is the worst thing that parliament could have done to the survivors,” she said.

“I feel devastated for those in particular who were anonymous and for those whose cult actually also submitted and now can see the names of members who submitted.

“This exactly demonstrates the complete lack of ability of government bodies to act and protect victims and whistleblowers … survivors are shocked and scared.”

The report included 39 recommendations for dealing with cults and supporting survivors. This included new legislation to criminalise group‑based coercion and to develop nationally consistent approaches to identifying and responding to group‑based coercion. It also called for support for Victoria police to establish a “clear internal pathway” for matters involving coercive high‑control groups.

The committee also recommended that the state government establish “a formal lived experience advisory body”, to address the impacts of coercive high‑control groups

Clare Heath-McIvor, from Survivors of Coercive Cults and High-Control Groups, said it was important that the recommendations were “belief-neutral”, with the report specifically recommending against introducing any legal definition of a cult.

“This is a vitally important recommendation that we fully support,” she said.

“No victim should have to prove their group is a cult before proving that group-based coercive control and abuse occurred, or that it mattered.

“Any group can be a cult – multi-level marketing cults, yoga cults, political cults and more all exist. Cults are not a phenomenon of belief, but coercive control and domination across multiple domains of life.”

australia.title: Rare moment humpback whale gives birth captured by drone off Australian coast – video
australia.snippet: A drone pilot has captured what is believed to be only the fourth complete humpback whale birth ever recorded on film anywhere in th...
australia.content:
A drone pilot has captured what is believed to be only the fourth complete humpback whale birth ever recorded on film anywhere in the world, and the first ever documented by drone. While conducting aerial observations of migrating humpback whales off the NSW north coast for the Organisation for the Rescue and Research of Cetaceans in Australia (Orrca), Alexander Forrest witnessed an adult female give birth in calm sea conditions, capturing the newborn calf's first moments of life, including its first breath and union with its mother

australia.snippet: This blog is now closed Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Specially designed Airbus completes marathon 24-hour...
australia.content:
Petrol back above $2 a litre and diesel at $2.40 in some cities

Luca Ittimani

Petrol is back above $2 a litre and diesel prices have hit $2.40 in some cities as fuel costs race upwards.

Oil prices have steadily risen since the US resumed strikes on Iran, with Brent crude up from about US$70 on 2 July to US$87 today, while the Australian government reduced its fuel excise discount by 16 cents a litre.

Service stations have passed the higher wholesale fuel prices on to customers.

Melbourne is facing diesel prices of $2.40 a litre today, up 66 cents from their June low of 173.9c/L, according to Motormouth. Canberra is at 238c/L, Brisbane is at 234.4, Adelaide at 233.7, Sydney 232.8, and 226.4 in Perth.

Unleaded petrol prices have risen to 204.1 cents a litre in Canberra. They’re at 195.6c/L in Melbourne, 195.2 in Brisbane, 192.6 in Adelaide and 191.1, in Sydney – the latter up from its June low of 152.2. Perth has seen the biggest jump, with unleaded at 196.6c/L today, up nearly 50 cents from the June low of 148.3.

    Welcome

What we learned, Wednesday 29 July

And that’s a wrap on our live coverage for the day.

Before we head off, let’s look at the day’s top headlines:

  • The former Victorian premier Daniel Andrews has issued a rare public statement paying tribute to his successor, Jacinta Allan, and declaring that Labor’s new leader, Ben Carroll, can win the state election in four months’ time.

  • Carroll also introduced a bill late on Wednesday to scrap group voting tickets to elect the state’s upper house.

  • The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, says no payments were made in relation to a growing corruption case involving members of the NSW Liberal party, insisting he is not a party to the proceedings. The NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) also resumed its examination of former Liberal staffer Dylan Whitelaw.

  • Inflation has dropped to 3.8% in the year to June, from 4% in the previous month, with lower than anticipated underlying price pressures weighing against the chance of another Reserve Bank interest rate hike.

  • South Australia police are investigating the deaths of a mother and toddler as a murder-suicide after their bodies were found in the ocean off the coast west of Port Macdonnell.

  • The Greens have renewed called for rent freezes as they say today’s inflation figures still reflect a cost of living reality that is too expensive for Australian households.

  • The federal agriculture minister, Julie Collins, has said the government is preparing for further H5 bird flu detections in Australian wildlife after “local transmission between birds may indicate that we will continue to see spread”. Conservationists have expressed fears for Kangaroo Island’s iconic Australian sea lion population, after H5N1 bird flu was detected in a greater crested tern at Seal Bay.

Thanks for sticking around, see you tomorrow morning!

Victoria to finally scrap group voting tickets to elect its upper house

Benita Kolovos

Rightwing provocateur Avi Yemini and anti-lockdown activist Monica Smit will no longer be able to use their “Free Palestine” and the “Save the Environment” parties to funnel preferences to One Nation and other conservative parties, with the new Victorian premier introducing legislation to parliament to scrap group voting tickets.

Ben Carroll on Wednesday afternoon announced that legislation had been introduced to parliament to abolish the system.

Under GVTs, voters can only choose one party above the line on the ballot paper, with their preferences then allocated by the party if it’s knocked out during counting. The system has allowed backroom deals between parties to flourish, enabling some candidates to get elected with only a minuscule number of primary votes.

Carroll said under the Electoral amendment (miscellaneous matters) bill 2026, a new above-the-line voting system will require voters to number at least five groups in order of preference. Those preferences will then flow to candidates in the order they appear below the line for each party or group.

In a YouTube video in April, Yemini said he had registered his party to “flow our preferences on to parties that want to free Palestine from Hamas” in the November poll.

Carroll said:

Fair elections are the bedrock of democracy, and we are delivering these reforms to ensure Victorians can be confident in their electoral processes. Victorians shouldn’t wake up after an election wondering how someone with only a handful of votes ended up in Parliament.

SA police officer allegedly stabbed in the neck and armed suspect shot in the leg

A South Australian police officer is in hospital with stab wounds to the neck after a confrontation with an armed man who was shot in the leg by police.

Police said they responded to multiple reports from the public of a knife-wielding man running on to Main North Road at Elizabeth East at about 11am.

The officer was transported to hospital and is receiving treatment for serious injuries. Police said they are providing appropriate support to her colleagues and family.

The suspect was also taken to hospital and is being treated for a gunshot wound. Police said his injuries are “not deemed to be life-threatening” and he will remain in police custody.

Acting Cmdr David O’Donovan praised the officers involved for their “courage, discipline and professionalism” during what he described as “an evolving and rapidly dangerous situation”.

Police have ruled out any further threat to the public or wider community.

Sarah Martin

One Nation faces being struck off in Queensland after failing to file audited financial statements

Pauline Hanson’s One Nation party faces being struck off in Queensland after failing its legal obligation to lodge audited financial statements with the state’s regulator.

The breach exposes Hanson and the New South Wales One Nation senator Sean Bell to financial penalties, with Hanson registered as president and Bell as secretary for the party in Queensland, where it is headquartered.

One Nation, which has been facing growing scrutiny of its finances as it has surged in popularity over the past year, has failed to lodge three years of audited financial reports.

Read more:

Penry Buckley

Rising Tide protesters interrupt address by NSW premier amid coalmine expansion proposal

Climate activists have interrupted an address by the NSW premier, Chris Minns, to protest a controversial coal expansion proposal currently being considered in the state.

The premier was giving the main address at the Committee for Economic Development’s (Ceda) State of the State series in Sydney this afternoon.

In a post on Instagram, climate protest group Rising Tide took responsibility for interrupting the event, with a video showing a protester attempting to hand the premier the NSW Net Zero Commission report, which has warned that extended or expanded coal mines are inconsistent with the state’s legislated climate targets. Rising Tide said:

We just tried to hand NSW Premier Chris Minns his government’s own Net Zero Commission report.

Yet the largest coal project proposed in NSW history, the HVO expansion project, is currently before the Independent Planning Commission. And just yesterday Chris Minns said he supported its approval.”

During his speech, Minns said the government was “taking heat from both sides of the political spectrum when it comes to energy policy”.

He defended his government’s support for coal and gas, saying “the easiest way of seeing diminishing support for renewable energy transition in New South Wales is if the lights start going out on a regular basis and bills rise even farther and faster than they currently are”.

In a statement, NSW police said officers were called to the event at a hotel in Martin Place, following reports two people had attempted to approach the stage.

Officers attached to Sydney City Police Area Command spoke to a man and a woman before they were directed to leave the venue, to which they complied. There will be no further police action.

‘We will continue to see spread’: authorities warn of further bird flu cases after local transmission confirmed

The federal agriculture minister, Julie Collins, has said the government is preparing for further H5 bird flu detections in Australian wildlife after “local transmission between birds may indicate that we will continue to see spread.”

There are currently 27 confirmed cases of H5 bird flu in Australia: 10 in Western Australia, 14 in South Australia, two in New South Wales and one in Queensland.

Speaking at a press conference in Sydney, Collins said that “while there remains no evidence of any mass mortality at this point in time, we do expect with this local transmission that there will be further detection”. She said:

States and territories will continue to undertake activities on the ground, particularly through shared costs, to manage the impact of the H5 bird flu.

Once it becomes established, what we do know from overseas, is that it is not able to be eradicated. So, what we will do is continue to monitor and evaluate and see where this disease is in Australia.

The Australian chief veterinary officer, Dr Beth Cookson, said it was “a concerning development” but “not unexpected”.

This news of some local transmission may mean we start to see wider spread among wild birds and other susceptible wildlife. This small shift in the situation will be very disappointing to many, but is certainly not an unexpected development as the last continent to detect H5 bird flu.

The government has confirmed there have been no detections in poultry or the wider agricultural sector. It said advice from the Australian Centre for Disease Control remains that risk to human health is low.

Petrol back above $2 a litre and diesel at $2.40 in some cities

Luca Ittimani

Petrol is back above $2 a litre and diesel prices have hit $2.40 in some cities as fuel costs race upwards.

Oil prices have steadily risen since the US resumed strikes on Iran, with Brent crude up from about US$70 on 2 July to US$87 today, while the Australian government reduced its fuel excise discount by 16 cents a litre.

Service stations have passed the higher wholesale fuel prices on to customers.

Melbourne is facing diesel prices of $2.40 a litre today, up 66 cents from their June low of 173.9c/L, according to Motormouth. Canberra is at 238c/L, Brisbane is at 234.4, Adelaide at 233.7, Sydney 232.8, and 226.4 in Perth.

Unleaded petrol prices have risen to 204.1 cents a litre in Canberra. They’re at 195.6c/L in Melbourne, 195.2 in Brisbane, 192.6 in Adelaide and 191.1, in Sydney – the latter up from its June low of 152.2. Perth has seen the biggest jump, with unleaded at 196.6c/L today, up nearly 50 cents from the June low of 148.3.

Jewish medical group details ‘increased politicisation’ in the health sector

Healthcare workers need to take caution in what they post to personal social media accounts, a peak body for Jewish medical practitioners warns.

AAP reports senior members of the Australasian Jewish Medical Federation have provided the royal commission into antisemitism with examples of multiple incidents in which people felt unsafe or doctors were rejected by patients because of their cultural identity.

The federation’s president, Jack Green, said the organisation “hardly ever” received reports of antisemitism before Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack on Israel and the subsequent conflict in Gaza.

“There was increased politicisation in the health sector, there were a lot of social media postings,” Green said of the shift.

There were a lot of increasingly distressed Jewish medical practitioners and they started contacting us.

Doctors became afraid to display symbols indicating their Jewish identity and, in one instance, an Israeli-Australian patient experienced significant distress seeing “overt political symbols” in a Northern Territory hospital, Green said.

Icac witness accepts former NSW Liberal minister did not have extramarital affair despite ‘shit sheet’ claim

Penry Buckley

Returning to the NSW Icac’s Operation Rosny hearing earlier, witness Dylan Whitelaw was cross-examined over a claim he repeated about a purported extramarital affair by the former NSW Liberal minister David Elliott.

The claims were in a document titled “David Elliott shit sheet” allegedly shared between members of the hard right factional group the Reformers.

Elliott’s lawyer, Bruce Levet, questioned the document which claimed that during the pandemic lockdowns, Elliott was photographed leaving the residence of another woman while his wife was undergoing treatment for cancer. Whitelaw accepted Levet’s submission that Elliott’s wife had treatment for cancer in 2012, not during the pandemic.

He agreed with Levet that he had not seen any photograph, saying he was not aware if “any specific photo” existed. “No one ever showed me,” said Whitelaw. Finally, they had this exchange:

Levet: “I suggest to you that no such affair occurred.”

Whitelaw: “I would accept that.”

Following today’s evidence, Elliott put out a statement reported by the Sydney Morning Herald, in which he strongly rejected any claims of an affair.

I reject all the accusations made by the young boy, Dylan, and his colleagues on the religious right of the Liberal Party.

As most of Sydney knows I’m a devoted husband of 30 years to a beautiful woman who doesn’t deserve to be treated like this by the party she has sacrificed so much for.

Needless to say I’m looking forward to the possibility of providing my own observations should the Commission see fit to invite me to give evidence.

Nick Visser

That’s all for me. Achol Arok will take things from here. Enjoy the arvo.

NSW says it won’t sell koala national park carbon credits to coal and gas companies

Lisa Cox

The NSW government says it will not sell any carbon credits generated by its planned Great Koala national park to coal and gas companies.

The government said today it had submitted the Great Koala national park to the Clean Energy Regulator for approval under a new carbon method that will allow state governments to earn credits by storing carbon dioxide in native forests on public land.

If approved, the government would cease logging within the park’s boundaries and move legislation to formally establish its long-promised Great Koala national park.

The Minns government wants the park accredited under the new method so that it can use revenue from the carbon credits to fund the park’s management.

But it has faced criticism from some environment groups who object to offsetting on public forests or hold concerns credits could be purchased to offset coal and gas projects.

The NSW environment minister, Penny Sharpe, said on Wednesday if the Clean Energy Regulator approves the project the state government will prioritise selling the ACCUs (Australian Carbon Credit Units) to “targeted manufacturing industries in NSW”. Sharpe said:

ACCUs from the Great Koala national park will not be able to be sold to coal and gas projects.

The Bob Brown Foundation said:

Today’s announcement ruling out trading Great Koala National forests for coal and gas does not rule out making those credits available to facilitate NSW’s biggest industrial emitters such as Port Kembla Steel and Tomago Aluminium.

Greens renew calls for rent freeze amid inflation data

The Greens say today’s inflation figures, which show inflation unexpectedly easing to 3.8%, still reflect a cost of living reality that is too expensive for Australian households.

The party said housing costs are driving inflation, and there should be a freeze on rents for 12 months and a moratorium on no-cause evictions during the ongoing fuel crisis.

Barbara Pocock, the Greens’ spokesperson for housing, said in a statement:

High inflation means that too many households are just one rent increase away from eviction or homelessness. A rent freeze and ban on evictions will give people more security in a cost of living and fuel crisis.

Households across the country are already doing it tough. They’re struggling to pay their rent and mortgages, as well as the cost of essentials, while they watch their wages go backwards. …

The Government must freeze rents and stop no cause evictions. They need to invest directly and at scale in good quality public housing and stop fiddling at the edges with things like the 5% deposit scheme, which actually pushes prices up to make the housing crisis worse.

Read more here:

Patrick Commins

Full scale of mortgage offset failures ‘completely unknown’, says Asic chair

Sarah Court, the Asic chair, at a press conference earlier this morning discussed the regulator’s latest report, which revealed banks’ “significant failures” when it came to managing mortgage offset accounts.

“We have found that banks are failing to deliver interest savings to many of their customers, costing millions of dollars a year in extra interest,” Court said.

The corporate regulator’s report revealed lenders paid $55m in compensation to 264,000 customers over two years to August 2025, and Court said the ultimate number will be higher.

It’s clear that the banks we surveyed may themselves not know the full extent of these issues. The amount of the potential losses to customers at this stage is completely unknown.

The Asic chair detailed some examples of the substantial and often hidden cost of these failures:

In one case, a customer paid more than $3,500 in extra interest in just over one month when their offset account was incorrectly de-linked by their bank.

In another example, two customers paid more than $17,000 in additional interest after the bank failed to inform their broker that the offset account needed to be relinked following refinancing.

Now, many of these failures went undetected until Asic started our work.

David Pocock is writing an illustrated children’s book about birds

Josh Butler

Federal senator David Pocock is writing a new book, a field guide for native birds geared toward children.

Pocock, the independent senator from the ACT, has declared an “advance from Penguin Random House Australia for book contract” on his parliamentary register interests.

Reached for comment, Pocock said he’d have more to say soon, but that it was an illustrated field guide for birds, in conjunction with a local ecologist.

Pocock is a noted wildlife fan, backing the gang gang cockatoo for Guardian Australia’s Bird of the Year poll in 2025.

Melissa Davey

Peak medical body says no need for high concentration medicinal cannabis

The president of the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners, Dr Michael Wright, says there is “no clinical need” for THC concentrations to be so high in the medicinal cannabis products available in Australia.

Guardian Australia reported that doctors are commonly prescribing high-dose medicinal cannabis containing up to four times the concentration of THC tested in clinical trials. There are adverse events being reported associated with these products, such as psychosis.

THC, or delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, is the main psychoactive ingredient of cannabis.

There is no upper limit for THC concentration allowed in medicinal cannabis products in Australia.

“Concentrations of up to 98% THC have been available to patients,” Wright said.

With the possible exception of palliative care, there’s no situation where such high doses of THC are warranted. High-THC products can heighten anxiety, create cannabis dependency, and in some cases lead to psychosis. The increase we’ve seen in hospital presentations for psychosis is deeply concerning.

According to TGA data, chronic pain and anxiety drive the majority of prescriptions.

This is despite research that has found medicinal cannabis is no more effective than placebo at reducing anxiety symptoms, and a 2018 review concluding there is low quality evidence that cannabis may be associated with small reductions in pain.

Wright said online providers are driving poor prescribing practices.

Online cannabis clinics operating as businesses create conflicts of interest, fragment care, and put patients at risk.

The problem is the vertically integrated, single-issue telehealth model, where patients often self-assess their eligibility for a predetermined treatment.

Penry Buckley

Further mention of purported Angus Taylor payments at NSW Icac

The NSW Icac’s Operation Rosny hearing has now concluded for the day. Before it finished, finished former Liberal staffer, Dylan Whitelaw, was asked again about purported payments by the federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, to the Reformers, who are being investigated by Icac.

This morning, Taylor has said he made no payments to the hard-right factional group after messages read out at the inquiry yesterday purported to show Taylor had agreed with Catholic Schools NSW CEO, Dallas McInerney, to make a one-off payment of $15,000 and a $3,000 monthly donation.

Counsel assisting, Juliet Curtin, had the following exchange with Whitelaw today:

Curtin: “That monthly retainer of $3,000, though, are you able to say whether that had anything to do with the increase that [Reformer-controlled lobbyist] Beckington received in its monthly retainer [from Catholic Schools NSW] from March 2021?”

Whitelaw: “Sorry, I don’t.”

Curtin: “Are you able to say whether there’s a connection between the monthly amount that Angus Taylor had indicated to Mr McInerney that he’s prepared to make and the corresponding increase, well, it appears to be an increase that happened at the same time in the amount that Catholic Schools New South Wales was paying to Beckington?

Whitelaw: “No, I wouldn’t be able to talk to that.”

Taylor is not accused of any wrongdoing.

Penry Buckley

Continued from previous post …

On Monday, the inquiry heard a phone call featuring Jean Nassif in which he allegedly claimed he had paid for David Chandler’s removal. He also allegedly claimed that “the fair trading minister is gonna to be one of my girls”.

The inquiry heard that two months after the call, the then Liberal premier, Dominic Perrottet, appointed Eleni Petinos as fair trading minister in a reshuffle. In July 2022, Chandler handed in his resignation following an investigation into his conduct that had been requested by Petinos, which later cleared him of any wrongdoing. The watchdog heard that evidence would determine if Nassif’s call was “an incidence of wishful thinking that serendipitously came to pass” or the result of work by the Reformers.

Spence, Perrottet and Petinos are not named in any allegations, and have not been accused of any wrongdoing.

On Tuesday the NSW Liberal leader, Kellie Sloane, said she had checked in on Petinos, who is on maternity leave. She has not asked Petinos to stand aside from shadow cabinet during the inquiry.

Penry Buckley

Inquiry hears about video allegedly circulated to damage building commissioner

Questioning by the NSW Icac of former Liberal staffer Dylan Whitelaw moved earlier to his time working in 2022 in the office of the then Liberal planning minister, Anthony Roberts.

One of the allegations Icac is investigating is whether members of the Reformers solicited or accepted donations from fugitive property developer Jean Nassif in exchange for the pursuit of outcomes including the removal of the then building commissioner, David Chandler.

Whitelaw has described an incident in which Roberts’ chief of staff, Christopher Spence, claimed to have a potentially damaging video of Chandler, with Spence saying he planned to give it to the then fair trading minister and current Liberal shadow minister, Eleni Petinos, to use in budget estimates.

Whitelaw says he is not aware if Spence spoke to Petinos about the video, saying they “were very close”. Asked if Spence had sought to circulate the video to bring about Chandler’s removal, Whitelaw told the inquiry Spence said words to the effect of: “We’ve just got to get rid of this guy”.

Whitelaw says he never saw the video, which he alleges included the imputation Chandler was racist, and included reference to a list of “dodgy” developers or certifiers that the building commissioner had passed on to banks. He says Spence never told him where he had received the video from.

Asked if he knew of Spence’s alleged plan to discredit Chandler at budget estimates “came to fruition”, Whitelaw says he does not, and he did not know why Petinos would want to have Chandler removed.

No, I don’t believe it did because I recall a subsequent conversation occurring … [Spence] walked into the office and said, ‘I can’t believe it, Eleni fucked it up’, excuse my language, or words to that effect.

Petinos is not accused of any wrongdoing.

Dfat investigating if any Australians affected by Japan quakes

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Dfat) is investigating if any Australians were affected by yesterday’s earthquakes in Japan.

A spokesperson for the agency said in a statement:

We are deeply saddened by the loss of life and damage in Japan resulting from the earthquake in Kyushu. Australians in the affected area should follow the advice of local authorities.

Australian officials are liaising with local authorities to determine whether any Australians have been affected. We stand ready to provide consular assistance.

At least 13 people were killed in the temblors and hundreds injured.

australia.title: Daniel Andrews says Ben Carroll ‘can win’ Victoria election in rare public statement
australia.snippet: Former leader shows support for new Victorian premier while paying tribute to Jacinta Allan Follow our Australia news live blog for lates...
australia.content:
Daniel Andrews has thrown his support behind Victoria’s new premier, Ben Carroll, saying he has what it takes to win November’s state election.

In a rare public statement on Wednesday, the former premier also paid tribute to Jacinta Allan, whom he handpicked to replace him as Labor leader when he resigned in September 2023.

Allan quit the top job on Tuesday morning, minutes before she was set to face a planned leadership spill brought on by Carroll. According to Carroll, he agreed to stand after a cross-factional delegation of MPs told him on Monday the premier had lost the confidence of the caucus. On his first full day as premier, Carroll announced legislation to abolish group voting tickets (GVTs), which are only used in Victoria, had been introduced to parliament.

The system has allowed backroom deals between parties to flourish, enabling some candidates to get elected with only a minuscule number of primary votes.

In his statement, Andrews said he first met Allan when he was the “most junior official at the ALP Head Office and she was the youngest candidate in a seemingly unwinnable Liberal stronghold in Bendigo”.

“Together, we worked to win that seat and for the next 25 years, to elect Labor governments and deliver a Labor agenda for working people,” Andrews said.

“There is no greater compliment in politics than to say someone lives their values – that has always been true of JA. For nearly three decades, she has been a champion for Bendigo, for workers, for women, for the future of Victoria.”

Andrews congratulated Carroll on his elevation, describing him as a “great campaigner who will take it up to the Liberal Party and One Nation”.

“Elections like this are won by a handful of votes in a handful of seats. I believe Premier Carroll and his team can win in November,” he said. “As he has rightly pointed out the stakes are high.”

He also expressed concern that Victoria could face cuts to service if the Liberals form government with the help of One Nation.

Another former Labor premier, Steve Bracks, said Allan had “no option” but to resign on Tuesday, and that Carroll would bring a “fresh approach”.

“He’ll market himself as not a fourth-term Labor leader, but as a new Labor leader … in a new term with a new set of policies and programs,” Bracks told ABC radio.

On Wednesday, Carroll said the GVT bill would require voters to number at least five groups in order of preference when voting for upper house candidates. Those preferences will then flow to candidates in the order they appear below the line for each party or group.

The changes means rightwing provocateur Avi Yemini and anti-lockdown activist Monica Smit would no longer be able to use their “Free Palestine” and the “Save the Environment” parties to funnel preferences to One Nation and other conservative parties.

Under GVTs, voters can only choose one party above the line on the ballot paper, with their preferences then allocated by the party if it’s knocked out during counting.

Carroll said “Victorians shouldn’t wake up after an election wondering how someone with only a handful of votes ended up in Parliament”.

Prior to Tuesday, speculation about a leadership spill had been building for months, fuelled by polling that suggested Labor would lose the November election, alongside Allan’s unpopularity and rising support for One Nation.

Allan’s leadership had also been dogged by allegations of corruption by the construction union working on the government’s Big Build of infrastructure, as she was the minister responsible at the time. While she apologised for criminal conduct that has been uncovered, she had also rejected calls for a royal commission, despite pleas from colleagues.

Carroll’s first act as premier was to announce he would hold a royal commission into the entire construction section.

He told reporters on Wednesday he had already asked the Department of Premier and Cabinet to start working on “exhaustive” terms of reference and confirmed the commission will look into the Labor government’s oversight of the Big Build.

“No stone [will be left] unturned,” Carroll said. “Whether it is top-tier contractors, subcontractors, labour hire, government, unions – these will be exhaustive terms of reference.”

But the opposition leader, Jess Wilson, has a claimed terms of reference written by the the government would be akin to a “cover up”.

“We’re concerned that it will not cover the links to the Labor party and who knew what, when in the union movement, what ministers knew [and] when,” she said, adding the opposition could go ahead with their own separate inquiry if they win the November election.

Carroll, meanwhile, also flagged the Suburban Rail Loop – a key project of Allan’s and Andrews’ – would also be discussed by cabinet.

He did not indicate whether the project would be reviewed. But when asked in question time about possibly breaking $14bn worth of contracts already signed for the SRL East section alone, which is forecast to cost up to $34.5bn, he said he was not in the business of cancelling contracts.

“That era is over,” Carroll said.

The new premier chose a Kmart store as the location for Wednesday’s press conference, in a nod to his eight years working at its Airport West store through high school and university.

world.title: Kenya investigating unexpected deaths of 15 elephants in national park
world.snippet: Potential toxic substance detected in several of 15 elephants found dead in Kenya’s Amboseli national park Officials are investigating th...
world.content:
Officials are investigating the deaths of 15 elephants over the past month in Kenya’s Amboseli national park.

The Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) said 10 of the elephants showed signs of partial paralysis before dying within two days.

The remaining five carcasses were too decomposed or had been scavenged, making it impossible to establish the cause of death, the wildlife authority said.

Most of those affected were female elephants and their calves, with only one male among the dead. The deaths happened in the Kimana sanctuary and Kuku ranch areas surrounding the park, officials said.

Kenya has previously recorded incidents of elephants being poisoned as a result of poaching and human-wildlife conflict.

Preliminary tests on samples collected from the elephants by a laboratory at the University of Nairobi detected a “potential toxic substance,” while separate analyses by a government laboratory were negative for the toxins tested. KWS said further tests are under way.

“Environmental investigations are also being undertaken, including the analysis of water sources and other potential environmental contaminants within the affected areas, to establish whether the elephants were exposed to a common source,” the authority said in a statement.

The authorities sought to reassure the public, saying there was no evidence the condition could be transmitted to humans.

Amboseli is world-renowned for its herds of elephants and its savannah landscapes, with Kilimanjaro visible across the border in Tanzania.

It is estimated there are about 2,000 elephants in the park.

With Associated Press and Agence France-Presse

world.title: Uganda begins emergency food handouts after 19 die from hunger
world.snippet: Government move follows months of drought and crop failures in Karamoja, with 1.5m people facing malnutrition Uganda has launched emergen...
world.content:
Uganda has launched emergency food relief distribution after at least 19 deaths from hunger were reported in an area of prolonged drought in the east of the country.

A crisis has been building in the Karamoja region of Uganda as crops have failed without the season’s expected rains, leaving the region’s 1.5 million people facing acute food shortages and rising malnutrition.

The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (Fews Net), a global mapping network designed to raise the alert on food security, reported the situation had deteriorated to a crisis across Karamoja.

In the first large-scale operation of its kind organised by the Ugandan government after the funding void left by aid cuts, authorities announced plans to distribute 9,400 tonnes of relief food over the next two months. The supplies were procured using a 45bn-shilling (£9m) emergency funding allocation, approved by parliament.

Sam Engola, minister for disaster preparedness and refugees, launched the aid distribution efforts at a primary school in Lodiko sub-county in Kaabong district on Wednesday.

“The president does not want to hear of anyone in Karamoja dying of hunger. I am here to supervise the distribution of this food to the end. I will ensure that everyone receives food. No one will be left behind,” Engola said.

Karamoja is experiencing its most severe dry spell in years. Farmers have lost crops since the last meaningful rainfall was recorded in April – the beginning of the planting season.

Angelina Nakiru, a 21-year-old mother of two in Rupa, about 5 miles from Moroto town in Karamoja, said she was struggling to feed her children after all her crops failed. Now she goes early each morning to join other women at a small-scale grinding mill where machines are used to crush rock into powder to wash out gold-bearing ore. The pay is meagre.

“The work is dusty and exhausting, but it is the only way I can earn money to buy a cup of maize and beans to feed the children,” Nakiru said.

“If I don’t, the children will sleep hungry. Other days when I fail to get the meagre income from the mill, we go to bed on empty stomachs,” she said.

“The situation is terrible. People are starving and dying due to hunger. The government must come to the rescue of the people.”

Health facilities report treating hundreds of children for severe malnutrition. A nutrition report published in June found nearly half of the population in Karamoja’s Kaabong and Kotido districts in a crisis situation.

Experts attribute the region’s recurring food insecurity and vulnerability to climate crisis shocks, environmental degradation such as deforestation and overgrazing, as well as poverty and low agricultural productivity.

In 2022, a devastating hunger crisis claimed more than 2,200 lives, according to figures from Uganda’s human rights commission body.

While emergency food aid is expected to provide short-term relief, the government said it remained committed to implementing long-term remedial measures with the recently approved Karamoja regional development plan, which is intended to strengthen communities’ resilience to drought.

John Baptist Lokii, minister for Karamoja, said: “The government will provide drought-resistant, disease-resistant and early-maturing seeds ahead of the next planting season.”

Agnes Kirabo, executive director of Uganda’s Food Rights Alliance (FRA), said the government was taking the lead on distribution as a necessity as much as a policy choice as the landscape of humanitarian aid had changed dramatically.

Following significant funding cuts, most notably from USAID, which previously had an annual budget of about $42.8bn (£32.bn), agencies such as the World Food Programme (WFP) have been forced to drastically scale back their aid.

In Uganda, the WFP has phased out food assistance for 63% of the refugee population, cutting off more than 1 million people from aid, and reducing rations to just 663,000 recipients.

“This transition should not be viewed solely as a reaction to aid cuts, but also as a positive shift towards nationally owned, sustainable development. Government leadership is a constructive move, provided it is part of a long-term strategy to establish durable national systems,” said Kirabo.

“Emergency food distribution is a life-saving measure, not a permanent solution. To break this cycle, we must address the root causes of food insecurity through structural reforms.”

The FRA, Kirabo said, wanted access to food to be made a fundamental human right and the government to turn its attention to water infrastructure and climate resilience. “Karamoja possesses adequate rainfall and water routes to achieve food self-sufficiency, but requires the political will to strategically invest in water infrastructure for production,” she said.

“Ultimately, the Karamoja hunger crisis is a governance crisis. The government’s leadership in this emergency is welcome, but it must be matched by the political will to implement the systemic changes required to permanently protect the people of Karamoja and Uganda from predictable, preventable hunger.”

world.title: Two Russian men jailed in Angola for terrorism and spying
world.snippet: The men were convicted over alleged plan to stage coup and organise deadly demonstrations over fuel prices last year Two Russian men have...
world.content:
Two Russian men have been found guilty by an Angolan court of terrorism and spying after being accused of planning a coup and helping to organise deadly demonstrations in the southern African country last year.

Lev Lakshtanov and Igor Ratchin were sentenced to eight and 11 years in jail respectively. They had denied the charges, claiming they were in Angola for cultural and business activities.

From 28-30 July 2025, a minibus taxi strike over fuel price hikes descended into riots and looting, in which 22 people were killed and more than 1,600 arrested according to official figures.

Angola’s security forces were accused of firing live ammunition at protesters; the government said its “progressive” use of force was justified. Human Rights Watch had previously said Angola employed “excessive force” when it used rubber bullets and teargas to break up a peaceful protest against rising fuel prices on 12 July 2025.

Angolan prosecutors said Lakshtanov and Ratchin wanted to influence next year’s presidential elections, including by funding Angola’s largest opposition party, the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola (UNITA), or by forcing a leadership change within the Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola (MPLA), which has ruled the country since independence from Portugal in 1975.

Prosecutors also claimed the men were linked to Africa Politology, a Russian disinformation and propaganda network that emerged from the Wagner mercenary group.

Africa Politology was taken over by Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) after the death of the Wagner chief Yevgeny Prigozhin in 2023, according to an investigation by media outlets including Forbidden Stories. Wagner was rebranded as Africa Corps and absorbed by Russia’s military.

Angola, whose economy is highly dependent on oil exports, has historically been close with Russia. During the cold war years of Angola’s 1975-2002 civil war, the Soviet Union and Cuba supported the MPLA, while the US and apartheid South Africa backed its opponents, including UNITA. However, Angola’s president, João Lourenço, has improved relations with the US and Europe since taking power in 2017.

In the last decade, Russia has increased its presence in Africa. The Wagner group and then Africa Corps have provided security for the Central African Republic’s president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra, since 2017.

In 2021, Wagner forces arrived in Mali to support the military junta. Africa Corps also backs the military regimes in neighbouring Niger and Burkina Faso. Since 2023, Russian troops have also been deployed in Equatorial Guinea, Libya and Sudan, according to a US Congress report.

Madagascar’s president, Michael Randrianirina, has also boosted ties with Russia since taking power in a coup in October 2025. There are Russians in his presidential guard and a weekly programme about Madagascar-Russia relations was launched earlier this month on national television.

Two Angolans were also tried alongside the Russians. The sports journalist Carlos Tomé received a two-year suspended prison sentence. Francisco de Oliveira, the secretary-general of UNITA’s youth wing, was acquitted.

Prosecutors have appealed against those sentences, according to the Portuguese news agency Lusa. Lakshtanov and Ratchin have also appealed against their sentences, but will remain in detention while the appeal is processed, according to Lusa.

Russia’s embassy in Angola did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Agence France-Press contributed to this report

world.title: MoD cancels army training in Kenya over powers to prosecute British soldiers
world.snippet: September exercise called off after Kenya raises concerns over funding and jurisdiction for criminal offences The British army has been f...
world.content:
The British army has been forced to cancel training for its troops in Kenya after the Kenyan government refused to ratify a bilateral defence agreement.

While the UK government wanted to renew the existing agreement, Kenyan lawmakers had sought changes to give local authorities greater powers to hold British soldiers accountable for any offences committed in the country.

According to the Kenyan news outlet the Daily Nation, the dispute centres on which cases Kenya will retain primary jurisdiction over, while the amount of money Britain pays Kenya to host the training camp has also been a sticking point.

The chair of the Kenyan national assembly’s defence, intelligence and foreign relations committee, Nelson Koech, said the two governments were “actively engaging to address these outstanding issues”.

As a result of the Kenyan government’s decision, a planned exercise involving the 1st Battalion the Duke of Lancaster’s Regiment, which was due to begin in September, has been cancelled.

A Ministry of Defence spokesperson said: “The UK highly values its relationship with Kenya, which is underpinned by mutual benefit, respect and cooperation. The UK-Kenya Defence Partnership is one of the great strengths of our relationship. Our joint training and operations with the Kenyan Defence Forces are keeping both Kenyan and British people safe.

“It is with regret that the necessary licences required to allow training to take place in Laikipia later this year have not been forthcoming. As a result, the planned training will now be conducted at an alternative location outside Kenya.”

Kenya also benefits from training of its own armed forces at BATUK, the British army base near Nanyuki, and the presence of British troops is valuable for the economy.

The MoD spokesperson added: “We recognise the disappointment this decision will cause for those who would have benefited from the economic activity generated by the exercise.”

They said the UK government remained “committed to our defence partnership with Kenya”, adding that the UK would “continue to engage closely with the Kenyan government to support the resumption of training in-country at the earliest appropriate opportunity”.

However, there has been sustained pressure from Kenyan people opposed to the British army’s continued presence. Last year, a report to the Kenyan parliament into the base alleged human rights violations, environmental destruction and sexual abuse by British soldiers.

The most high-profile case linked to the base is the death of Agnes Wanjiru, in which a British soldier has been charged with murder. Kenya has retained jurisdiction in the case and an extradition hearing is due to take place in November. Robert Purkiss denies the single charge of murder.

Legal proceedings had stalled since Wanjiru’s death in 2012, but advanced under John Healey’s tenure as defence secretary. As shadow defence secretary, he had called on the previous government to do more to progress the case.

Koech said the committee had called for “stronger accountability measures, including jurisdiction over serious offences, enhanced protection for local communities, and implementation of recommendations arising from the BATUK inquiry”.

world.title: Health worker monitored for Ebola in London hospital after working in DRC
world.snippet: UK resident was evacuated from Democratic Republic of the Congo where there is an outbreak of the disease A humanitarian worker is being ...
world.content:
A humanitarian worker is being monitored at a specialist hospital in London after potential exposure to the Ebola virus.

The UK resident was medically evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) where the worker had been treating patients with the disease, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said.

UKHSA said the person was evacuated as a “highly precautionary measure”, adding: “The individual is not currently displaying any symptoms and remains well, but as a precautionary measure they have been evacuated on a flight chartered solely for the evacuation.

“They are now being assessed and monitored in isolation by infectious disease specialists at a London hospital.”

The agency said the incubation period of Ebola ranges from two to 21 days and the individual will be closely monitored and is required to isolate throughout this period.

There are no confirmed cases of Ebola in the UK and the risk to the general public remains low.

Richard Pebody, the director of epidemic and emerging infections at the UKHSA, said: “This individual has been transferred out of an abundance of caution and we’re pleased they remain well.”

Last month, a patient suspected of having the Ebola virus at a Glasgow hospital tested negative.

Precautionary measures were taken after the patient was admitted to the Queen Elizabeth University hospital.

An outbreak of the disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda in May was declared a public health emergency of international concern by the World Health Organization (WHO).

The virus is transmitted to people from wild animals and then spreads in the human population through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs or other bodily fluids of infected people and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding or clothing.

According to WHO, symptoms can include fever, fatigue, malaise, muscle, pain, headache and sore throat. These are followed by vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, rash, and symptoms of impaired kidney and liver functions.
